newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco cos seek to limit Florida trial jury.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco cos seek to limit Florida trial jury.

text.p: R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. Wednesday sought to exclude anyone who may believe they or a relative had suffered harm as a result of smoking from the jury that will hear Florida's $1-billion lawsuit against the tobacco industry.

A verdict rendered by a jury that included such a person "would be tainted not only legally, but forever would be subject to criticism," Reynolds attorney Robert Weber told Palm Beach Circuit Judge Harold Cohen.

Weber said anyone who fit the profile of a member of the class in a Miami class-action lawsuit known as Engle v R.J. Reynolds should be excluded from the jury that will hear Florida's Medicaid lawsuit, which seeks to recoup the costs of treating sick smokers.

In the Engle suit, Miami attorneys Stanley and Susan Roseblatt are seeking to recover millions of dollars in damages for all "Florida residents who had suffered or died from diseases and medical conditions caused by their addiction to cigarettes that contained nicotine."
Howard Engle, a Miami physician, is the lead plaintiff in the lawsuit that bears his name. He blames a lifetime of cigarette smoking for the asthma that he developed at age 50.

The case had been scheduled to go to trial in September, but now is expected to begin in December or January. The Rosenblatts are involved in another high profile tobacco case -- in which flight attendants are suing over secondhand smoke in airline cabins -- now on trial in Miami.

The motion to exclude Engle class members and relatives from the Florida tobacco case was filed with Cohen as he finished another day of pre-screening potential jurors for financial or health problems that would make serving on a trial of six months or longer a hardship.
To date, Cohen has found 104 people who may qualify to sit on the six-member jury or as one of the nine alternates for Florida's lawsuit. Jury selection began Aug. 1.
Peter Bleakley, a Philip Morris attorney, said tobacco attorneys were concerned that people with a vested interest in a "verdict favorable to the (state) may make it to the jury."
One tobacco company attorney pointed out that some of the potential jurors may not even realize that they were included in the Engle lawsuit.

Robert Montgomery, an attorney representing Florida, agreed there was a potential problem but said it could be handled during voir dire, when attorneys for both sides will question potential jurors to weed out the pool.
